summaries.headline: Startup Targets AI's Accuracy Problem in Diagrams
summaries.summary: AI startup F13 has raised $5 million to build models that generate precise, editable vector graphics for scientific diagrams, charts and educational materials rather than the stylized but often inaccurate output of general-purpose image generators. The company says its "data-faithful" approach preserves correct proportions, data and layout specifications, producing scalable graphics users can edit and iterate on rather than regenerate from scratch, with early access now open ahead of a public launch. For districts and curriculum developers relying on AI-generated visuals for instructional content, the distinction between an image that looks right and one that is factually correct carries real classroom stakes.

summaries.headline: Startup Targets the Post-Beginner English Gap
summaries.summary: Glite has launched an AI-powered app aimed not at beginners but at the roughly one billion intermediate and advanced English learners who can pass an exam but still struggle to follow a film without subtitles or speak confidently in a meeting. The app draws on a database of more than three million test-takers and 140 million data points to map what individual learners know and personalize what comes next, arriving as UNESCO projects a shortfall of 44 million teachers globally by 2030. For district leaders serving multilingual families and staff, tools built to close the "conversational but not fluent" gap may prove more relevant than yet another beginner language app.

summaries.headline: AI Test-Prep Startup Triples Valuation in Year
summaries.summary: Arivihan, a two-year-old AI-powered learning platform targeting tier-II and rural students preparing for Class 12 boards and NEET, is raising Rs 96 crore ($10 million) in a Series A round co-led by Accel and Prosus, pushing its valuation to roughly Rs 570 crore. That's a 3.3x jump from the Rs 171 crore valuation in its pre-Series A round just 15 months ago, with revenue climbing nearly 14.8x to Rs 3.14 crore in FY25. The rapid back-to-back funding signals investor confidence in AI-driven coaching and doubt-solving tools as a scalable answer to coaching-center gaps in smaller cities, even as the startup's actual student outcomes remain untested at scale.

summaries.headline: Lawmakers Revisit Funding Fix That Saved Morrisville Schools
summaries.summary: Pennsylvania's House Policy Committee will visit Morrisville High School this week to review how a state funding boost has affected the district, which warned last year it might have to close entirely. The $3.5 million infusion, secured in July through a new funding formula and made permanent to the district's base budget, came after House Majority Democrats and Senate Democrats targeted chronically underfunded districts for relief. The roundtable with administrators — examining how funds are being spent now and how they'll shape instruction going forward — signals that lawmakers see this as a test case for whether targeted state investment can stabilize districts on the brink, with implications for how similar funding formulas might be applied elsewhere.

summaries.headline: ILA Names New Leadership for Reading Teacher Journal
summaries.summary: The International Literacy Association has appointed a new editorial team to helm The Reading Teacher, one of the field's longstanding peer-reviewed publications for literacy educators. The leadership change signals a transition point for a journal that shapes how reading research reaches classroom practice across K-6 settings. For literacy coaches and curriculum leaders who rely on the publication to bridge research and instruction, the new editorial direction will be worth watching in the coming issues.

summaries.headline: Alexandria Expands Teacher-Led Math Coaching Model
summaries.summary: Alexandria City Public Schools is scaling its enVision Math model lesson program to every school in the division, using a Virginia Department of Education Mathematics Innovation Grant awarded in February to fund the expansion. The approach has teachers observe live math instruction in Alexandria classrooms, then work with colleagues and expert trainers to unpack instructional strategies and plan how to apply them, building on curriculum the division already uses from kindergarten through Algebra 2. Betting on peer observation and cross-school collaboration rather than one-off training days signals a district-wide push for instructional consistency that other divisions chasing math recovery may want to watch.

summaries.headline: UK Regulator Finds EdTech Vendors Confused on Data Roles
summaries.summary: The UK's Information Commissioner's Office audited 28 EdTech providers spanning management information systems, safeguarding tools, and learning platforms, issuing 596 compliance recommendations across the sector. The core problem: nearly 70% of providers correctly identified as data processors for their core product were also acting as data controllers for secondary uses like product development, analytics, and AI training, without recognizing the shift in legal obligations that status change triggers. For district leaders vetting vendors, the findings signal that contract language alone won't surface these blind spots — procurement teams need to ask pointed questions about exactly what happens to student data beyond the advertised service.

summaries.headline: Serbia Grounds Media Literacy Push in New Data
summaries.summary: Education and media researchers have released new findings meant to guide Serbia's media literacy initiatives, shifting the conversation from anecdote to evidence. The research, tied to Council of Europe-backed efforts, aims to give policymakers and educators a clearer picture of where students and schools stand on navigating misinformation and digital content. For a field often driven by urgency rather than data, the move signals a broader push to make media literacy programming measurable and accountable rather than assumed effective.

summaries.headline: Chicago Voters Pick First Elected Board President
summaries.summary: Chicago voters will choose the city's first directly elected school board president on Nov. 3, ending more than 30 years of mayoral control over the position. Four candidates are vying for the unpaid but influential role: CTU-backed Hilario Dominguez, who wants to expand preschool access and push the state for more funding; sitting board member Jessica Biggs, who has consolidated support from SEIU Local 73 and former Emanuel-era officials around fiscal stability; and attorney Victor Henderson, who is emphasizing student achievement and fiscal responsibility while backed by Urban Prep's charter network. The race has drawn millions in campaign contributions and competing union endorsements, signaling that whoever wins will inherit both a powerful bully pulpit and a deeply divided coalition to manage across 20 other board members.

summaries.headline: Consumer Panel Rejects EdTech's "Guaranteed Placement" Defense
summaries.summary: A Punjab consumer commission ordered Bengaluru-based Eduinx Education Services to refund the full Rs 84,960 fee to an MBA graduate who enrolled in its AI Product Management course after being promised "100% guaranteed placement" but never landed a job. The company argued the guarantee only covered career prep and employer outreach, not final hiring, and pointed to interview opportunities the graduate had turned down outside his preferred cities, but the commission found the firm failed to prove it had actually delivered on its advertised commitment, awarding an additional Rs 15,000 in compensation and costs. As districts and families increasingly turn to edtech platforms promising job outcomes, the ruling signals that marketing language like "guaranteed placement" carries real legal weight, not just recruiting appeal.

summaries.headline: Vendor Touts AI Bullying Detection for Schools
summaries.summary: AVer, a video technology company, is marketing new AI-powered camera software that claims to detect bullying incidents in real time as part of broader school safety systems. The announcement offers no independent research, pilot data, or third-party validation of detection accuracy, false-positive rates, or privacy safeguards. District leaders evaluating AI surveillance tools should treat vendor claims about behavioral detection with the same scrutiny applied to any unproven ed-tech pitch, particularly given the stakes around student privacy and disciplinary consequences.

summaries.headline: School Screenings Flag Depression in Nearly 1 in 3 Students
summaries.summary: Journey Mental Health, which partners with nine school districts across south central Wisconsin, screens more than 4,000 middle and high school students for mental health concerns each year. About 30% screen positive for depression, traumatic stress, or suicidal ideation, according to school and community outreach manager Julia Stanley, who emphasized the screenings are designed to connect kids with coping skills rather than serve as diagnoses. Embedding screening in the school day sidesteps the transportation, insurance, and access barriers that keep many students from getting help otherwise, underscoring how schools have become a primary entry point for identifying mental health needs early.

summaries.headline: Philippines Weighs 10,000 New School Counselor Jobs
summaries.summary: Philippine education officials are considering creating 10,000 new guidance counselor positions in response to a rise in school violence incidents. The proposal aims to strengthen student mental health support systems that advocates say have been stretched thin as behavioral and safety concerns mount in classrooms. The move signals a broader recognition that staffing gaps in student support services can leave schools reactive rather than preventive when it comes to identifying at-risk students before incidents escalate.

summaries.headline: OpenAI Pushes for Global AI Safety Standards
summaries.summary: OpenAI is calling for a US-led international effort to create shared technical standards for frontier AI, covering capability testing, risk assessment, incident reporting and human oversight of increasingly automated AI research. The proposal stops short of licensing or mandatory pre-release reviews, leaving individual governments to decide how—or whether—to write these standards into national law, and it leans on existing national AI safety institutions rather than creating a new global regulator. For district leaders watching AI policy shape the tools entering classrooms, this signals that federal and international guardrails on AI development are still taking form, with vendors themselves helping write the rulebook.

summaries.headline: Early Years AI Use Outpaces Training and Guidance
summaries.summary: Early years educators are adopting AI for admin work at a fast clip, with a Tapestry survey finding 46% used AI tools in the past six months, up from 33% the year before, and 66% reporting time savings on paperwork and parent communications. Only a third have received any guidance on using AI for admin tasks, just 21% of users have had formal AI training, and majorities cite concerns over accuracy (62%) and safeguarding or data protection (53%). Settings are embedding AI into daily practice faster than they're building the policies, training, and safeguards to manage it responsibly.

summaries.headline: Unions Demand Funding Clarity on New Vocational GCSEs
summaries.summary: The UK's Department for Education is rolling out new vocational GCSEs as part of a broader push to introduce technical subjects starting at age 14, but teachers' unions say critical questions about funding and workload remain unanswered. Unions are pressing the government to clarify how schools will pay for new curriculum development, staff training, and materials without additional workload falling on already-stretched teaching staff. Until DfE provides concrete funding commitments, district and school leaders face the familiar challenge of implementing policy mandates with resource questions still open.

summaries.headline: Teens Fill Financial Literacy Gap at Libraries
summaries.summary: A group of New Jersey teenagers has developed financial literacy kits now being distributed to public libraries throughout the state, giving community members hands-on tools to build money management skills outside the classroom. The student-led initiative reflects growing recognition that financial education often falls through the cracks in traditional K-12 curricula, even as more states move to mandate it before graduation. Libraries stepping in as delivery points signals an opportunity for districts to partner with community institutions on skills that schools alone haven't consistently taught.

summaries.headline: National Literacy Month Spotlights Third-Grade Reading Stakes
summaries.summary: National Literacy Month arrives this September with its usual reminder that third-grade reading proficiency remains one of the most reliable predictors of high school graduation and long-term academic success. The observance frames literacy as a workforce and civic issue as much as an academic one, linking reading comprehension to job access, healthcare navigation, and financial management in adulthood, while also flagging digital literacy as a growing extension of basic reading skills. For district leaders, the monthlong push offers a low-cost entry point for community partnerships — library cards, volunteer tutoring, book donations — that can reinforce literacy efforts without competing for scarce instructional budget.

summaries.headline: Startup Launches 11 EdTech Tools for Young Learners
summaries.summary: ShikshaNext has announced 11 new EdTech and AI products aimed at children ages 4 to 10, rolled out under its EdTech ScaleX and EdTech Accelerator initiatives. The announcement offers no independent data on classroom testing, learning outcomes, or district adoption, leaving the actual instructional value of these tools unverified. District leaders evaluating early-childhood AI products should look past launch announcements for evidence of efficacy before considering procurement.

summaries.headline: Wyoming's Top Court Splits on School Funding Case
summaries.summary: The Wyoming Supreme Court partly affirmed and partly reversed a lower court ruling that found the state chronically and unconstitutionally underfunded public schools, siding with the Wyoming Education Association and eight districts on core funding mechanics while pulling back on some remedies. Justices agreed the Legislature violated equal protection and students' fundamental right to adequate education by failing to account for inflation and true teacher salary costs, but reversed mandates requiring statewide funding for student computers, nutrition services and school resource officers, and rejected a required statewide facilities assessment, leaving those decisions to legislative discretion. The ruling lands as lawmakers are already recalibrating the funding model through a regular update cycle, and Gov. Mark Gordon's call for a "durable, transparent and constitutionally sound system" signals the political pressure to avoid another round of litigation over the same fundamental questions.

![](https://i0.wp.com/gazettenet.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/DSC_1943-scaled.jpg?fit=1200%2C800&ssl=1)State Sen. Joanne Comerford comments on purported inequities between Eastern and Western Massachusetts cities and towns. /ANTHONY CAMMALLERI / Staff Photo Credit: ANTHONY CAMMALLERI / Staff Photo

NORTHAMPTON — With the state preparing for a rare reexamination of how it pays for public education, state Sen. Jo Comerford is calling on Northampton residents and officials to make their voices heard, pushing for changes to a funding formula she says shortchanges many western Massachusetts communities.

The senator addressed inequities in formulas that dictate funding distribution of state school and infrastructure aid during a legislative update to the City Council at its Sept. 17 meeting, where she also outlined some of the Legislature’s financial and legislative achievements and goals for the city.

In the fiscal 2027 budget Gov. Maura Healey signed July 16, legislators agreed to revive the Foundation Budget Review Commission to examine Chapter 70, the K-12 funding formula that calculates how much state aid goes to each municipality and regional school district. The commission, expected to meet in October, will study how the state can address rising education costs, particularly special education, student transportation, personnel and employee health care.

“I’m begging you to be active. This commission will have hearings here — we’re going to fight to have the hearings here. I want you to pack the rooms,” Comerford said. “I want Northampton to be more present; I want you to be present in the foundation budget. This is once in 15 years … it means working as a city, galvanizing the public. I am going to file fewer bills this year so that I can organize to shake up the Foundation Budget Review Commission.”

Discussing some of the hurdles she faces when it comes to securing state funds for Northampton, Comerford mentioned the Chapter 70 formula. She argued that the formula does not work for rural communities, noting that districts with shrinking enrollments often pay more than they receive.

“Think of Chapter 70 as a big clamshell, where half of it is what the state gives Northampton and the other half of it is what the state tells Northampton it can and should pay,” Comerford said. “The top of the clamshell hasn’t been opened in 10 years \[and\] the bottom in 18 years. This is the moment.”

The commission last met in 2015, when it recommended changes to the state’s school funding formula that were estimated at the time to require roughly $432 million in additional Chapter 70 aid, largely to better account for employee health insurance and special education costs.

Comerford added that while the state’s 2019 Student Opportunity Act focused funding allocations on urban school districts facing high rates of poverty, it often overlooked more rural school districts in western Massachusetts. She explained that Franklin and Hampshire county school districts have slowly declining enrollment and are facing “death by a thousand cuts.”

School funding isn’t the only area of inequity Comerford highlighted last week. She said the state’s payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (PILOT) program, which offers cities and towns payments for state-owned land that falls into certain categories, uses a funding formula based on land values. Because land in eastern Massachusetts is typically more valuable than in western Massachusetts, cities and towns in this area receive less in PILOT funding.

“It’s wild — it’s like a moral abomination of a formula. It asks that Northampton’s land be seen as relative to Nantucket beaches,” Comerford said of the PILOT formula. “Of course, that’s bananas. We don’t have the land values, but that’s how we apportion state funding.”

Pointing to what she called similar inequities in grant and Chapter 90 infrastructure funding allocations between eastern and western Massachusetts, Comerford went on to explain that residents and local officials have to be loud to remind Beacon Hill of their region.

“The narrative that many people say is that Boston doesn’t care about us. That’s not true. The harder truth is that we just need to be in the room in order for them to think of us at all,” Comerford said. “We need to flex our muscles continually, because every time I look around, there’s an abominable piece of policy or a ridiculous budget line that’s just not going to be equitable for us.”

The Jersey City Board of Education (BOE) unanimously approved (9-0) a resolution calling on the state to review their school funding formula to assess its impact “on high-need school districts located within rapid development municipalities” at last week’s meeting.

![](https://cdn.hudsoncountyview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Jersey-City-BOE-e1790179941562.png) Screenshot via Facebook Live.

By John Heinis/Hudson County View

“Since 2018, the State has reduced support for the Jersey City Public Schools Adequacy Budget while simultaneously increasing local tax effort, the District continues to experience a significant shortfall in funding essential to ensure students a thorough and efficient education,” [the resolution](https://go.boarddocs.com/nj/jcps/Board.nsf/Public?open&id=policies) says.

“District revenue analyses reflect that in School Year 2017-2018 state aid exceeded $400 million, while the local tax levy was approximately $117 million; and currently, the local tax levy exceeds $530 million, while state aid no longer provides aid to support the SFRA Adequacy Budget and overall state aid has declined to approximately $125 million.”

[![](https://cdn.hudsoncountyview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aponte-Lipski-ad.png)](https://apontelipski.com/)

The action reflects growing concern that measures of municipal wealth and rising property values may not fully capture the educational and socioeconomic realities of students attending urban public schools in communities experiencing significant redevelopment.

Since the implementation of S-2, the state school funding formula, and related funding changes, Jersey City has experienced significant reductions in recurring state aid while increasing local tax effort to maintain educational programs and services.

“Jersey City Public Schools serves approximately 27,000 students, many of whom face challenges associated with poverty, language barriers, housing insecurity, and other educational disadvantages,” said Board President Noemí Velazquez.

“While Jersey City has experienced tremendous growth and development, the needs of the students in our classrooms have not diminished. Our resolution calls for a thoughtful review of the funding formula to ensure that student need remains at the center of school funding decisions.”

Among other issues, the Jersey City BOE has asked state lawmakers to examine:

• The treatment of local fair share calculations;

• The continuing impact of S-2 aid reductions on high-need urban districts; • The adequacy of weighting factors for economically disadvantaged students, multilingual learners, and students with concentrated educational needs;

• The relationship between aggregate municipal wealth indicators and actual district fiscal capacity; and

• Potential legislative or regulatory changes that would ensure equitable funding outcomes for similarly situated districts throughout New Jersey.

“This resolution is not about seeking special treatment for any one district. It is about ensuring that school funding policies accurately reflect student needs and the realities faced by districts educating large numbers of high-need students,” Velazquez added.

“We welcome the opportunity to work with state leaders and stakeholders to identify solutions that support educational equity for all New Jersey children.”

The school board also encouraged the state legislature and Department of Education to conduct hearings, listening sessions, and stakeholder meetings with districts confronting these challenges in order to develop informed policy recommendations.

local_articles.summary: Underly calls for changes to Wisconsin school funding in State of Education Address  Daily Dodge
local_articles.full_content:

![](https://dailydodge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Underly-768x628.jpg)

MADISON — Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly called for changes to the way the state funds public schools Wednesday, arguing that districts have become too reliant on local referendums to cover operating costs.

During her 2026 State of Education Address at the Wisconsin State Capitol, Underly said Wisconsin is at an “inflection point” and urged residents and policymakers to reconsider how the state pays for public education.

“This is our year to act,” Underly said. “We are at an inflection point and we must decide: Are we going to be part of the generation that allows the status quo to continue? Or are we going to be the generation that chooses to change?”

Underly used the address to connect public education with the nation’s 250-year democratic tradition, arguing that strong schools are important to preparing future generations of citizens and workers.

She also focused much of her speech on school finances, saying the current funding system does not provide districts with predictable and sustainable resources as costs rise.

Underly pointed to the prevalence of local school referendums as evidence of the problem. She said more than 90% of Wisconsin school districts have gone to referendum at least once during the past nine years to seek additional funding.

“The formula used for funding our schools, for years, has failed our children, schools, and entire communities,” Underly said.

Referendums allow school districts to ask local voters for authority to raise additional money beyond existing state-imposed limits. Underly argued that districts have increasingly had to rely on those votes to maintain operations and pay teachers.

She said that reliance can place additional pressure on communities and property taxpayers while creating uncertainty for school districts.

“Record numbers of referendums put pressure on communities, pit neighbors against neighbors and turn schools into casualties of partisan politics instead of the pride of their communities,” Underly said.

The superintendent did not limit her address to funding. She described public education as an institution that has helped sustain Wisconsin communities and American democracy, and she called on the state to continue investing in schools for future generations.

Underly ended the address by comparing that responsibility to extending a ladder to the next generation rather than benefiting from past investments and then withdrawing support.

“We can pull the ladder up behind us,” Underly said. “We can force the next generation to make do with less. We can allow the institutions that bind our communities together to erode, one decision at a time. Or we can choose differently.”
